fact: Woensel is first mentioned in a document from 1107; it was a large village with its own church district.
From 1817 until 1920 the coat of arms of Woensel was three golden horns on a blue shield.

The Oude Toren on the Oude Torenstraat is all that is left of Woensel's medieval church of St. Peter: a 15th-century brick tower whose spire was renewed in 1801, a rijksmonument (national monument number 14654) since 1972.
After the 1920 merger Philips grew fast and needed homes for its workers; Woensel-West was built for them between the 1930s and the 1950s.
The world head office of Philips stood on the Boschdijk in Woensel until Philips decided in 1997 to move to Amsterdam.

On 18 September 1944 American paratroopers coming from Son fought their way through Woensel; two German guns on the Woenselsestraat fired at them, and the soldiers reached the city centre around noon.
Woensel General Cemetery holds about 680 Commonwealth war graves, most of them of airmen.
Most of Woensel was built between 1950 and 1990; because it grew so big it was split into two districts, Woensel-Noord and Woensel-Zuid.
Winkelcentrum Woensel opened in 1971, with parachutists and hot-air balloons; it is now being rebuilt as part of the city's Stadshart Woensel plan.
Until 1 January 1920 Woensel was an independent municipality; then it merged into Eindhoven together with Strijp, Stratum, Tongelre and Gestel en Blaarthem.
One theory about the name Eindhoven is that it meant the last hoves (farm plots) on the land of Woensel; another theory links the name to the stream the Gender.
